name: Chang'e 2 (extended mission asteroid flyby)
rocket: Long March 3C (original 2010 lunar launch; not part of the modeled trajectory below)
payload: Chang'e 2 orbiter (2,480 kg at original lunar launch)
significance: After completing its primary lunar mapping mission, Chang'e 2 was redirected on an extended trajectory to test China's deep-space tracking and navigation capability beyond the Moon, with a flyby of near-Earth asteroid 4179 Toutatis as a low-cost bonus science target. On 13 December 2012 it passed within roughly 3.2 km of Toutatis (an estimated 1.9-3 km from the surface), making China the fourth space agency (after NASA, ESA, and JAXA) to conduct a close asteroid encounter, using repurposed lunar-orbiter hardware never designed for the task. Its roughly 400 images, at resolutions better than 3 meters, gave the highest-resolution look at Toutatis to date. The flyby revealed Toutatis to be an elongated, "peanut-shaped" contact binary about 4.75 km long, with a rubble-pile structure, boulders, an 800-meter depression, and a complex tumbling (non-principal-axis) rotation, data later used to refine impact-risk models for tumbling near-Earth objects.
statusNote: China's first probe to leave Earth-Moon space, during an extended mission tacked onto what began as a lunar orbiter (launched 2010-10-01, not modeled here -- lunar-orbit trajectories are a different regime this simulator doesn't model). This entry begins where the interplanetary extension actually starts: departure from lunar orbit toward Sun-Earth L2 on 2011-06-08 (approximated as departing from Earth, since the Moon's position is indistinguishable from Earth's at heliocentric scale), L2 arrival 2011-08-25, an L2 loiter (reusing the same trajectory-type ESCAPADE uses) until departure 2012-04-15, then on to asteroid 4179 Toutatis, flyby 2012-12-13 at an extraordinarily close 770 m -- the actual GA-chain machinery isn't invoked for this pass since Toutatis's mass is far too small for a meaningful gravity assist; four trajectory-correction maneuvers during this leg aren't separately modeled either. Spacecraft continued outward afterward and remains in a heliocentric orbit; not tracked further.
